questions.title: Teichoic acid is absent from the Gram-negative cell wall
questions.question: Cell wall of gram-negative bacteria contains the following EXCEPT ?

explanations.A: Correct. This is the false statement, so it is the EXCEPT answer. Teichoic acid is a component threaded through the thick peptidoglycan wall of Gram-positive bacteria specifically; Gram-negative bacteria lack it entirely.
explanations.B: Incorrect (genuine component, not the EXCEPT). Lipopolysaccharide (LPS) is carried on the Gram-negative outer membrane.
explanations.C: Incorrect (genuine component, not the EXCEPT). The Gram-negative wall does contain peptidoglycan, though as a thin layer compared with the thick Gram-positive wall.
explanations.D: Incorrect (genuine component, not the EXCEPT). The outer membrane, carrying LPS and enclosing a periplasmic space, is a defining Gram-negative structure.

questions.learning_objective: Identify teichoic acid as absent from the Gram-negative cell wall, while correctly recognising LPS, peptidoglycan and the outer membrane as genuine components.

questions.title: Lipid A is a Gram-negative cell wall component
questions.question: Lipid A is a cell wall component of ?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Gram-positive bacteria have no outer membrane and therefore no LPS, and no Lipid A, in their cell wall at all.
explanations.B: Correct. Lipid A is the lipid anchor of lipopolysaccharide (LPS), embedded in the outer membrane that is part of the Gram-negative cell envelope. It is Lipid A specifically that triggers the host inflammatory cascade when released, the toxic component of endotoxin.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Fungal cell walls are composed of chitin and glucans, not lipopolysaccharide -- Lipid A is a bacterial, not fungal, structure.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Viruses are not cells and have no cell wall of any kind, Lipid A included.

questions.learning_objective: State that Lipid A is a Gram-negative cell wall component, rejecting Gram-positive, fungal and viral attribution.

questions.title: Ribosomes are the site of bacterial protein synthesis
questions.question: Sites of protein synthesis in bacteria is ?

explanations.A: Correct. Bacterial (70S) ribosomes are the site of protein synthesis, translating messenger RNA into protein. During active synthesis, several ribosomes attach simultaneously to one mRNA strand, forming a polysome. This 70S-ribosome, polysome-forming behaviour is a standard testable feature of bacterial protein synthesis.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Mesosomes are cytoplasmic membrane invaginations with a respiratory and division-related role, not the site of protein synthesis.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Inclusion granules are reserved-nutrient storage structures, unrelated to protein synthesis.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The chromosome carries the genetic template (DNA) that is transcribed into mRNA, but protein synthesis itself is physically carried out at the ribosome, not the chromosome.

questions.learning_objective: Identify ribosomes as the site of bacterial protein synthesis, distinct from mesosomes, inclusion granules and the chromosome.

questions.title: The flagellum is protein in nature
questions.question: Which of the following is true regarding flagellum ?

options.D: Helps in bacterial adherence to host cells

explanations.A: Incorrect. The flagellum is a long, thin, whip-like structure, not a short, rigid one -- "short, rigid" better describes a fimbria/pilus, not a flagellum.
explanations.B: Incorrect. LPS (lipopolysaccharide) is a Gram-negative outer-membrane component, unrelated to flagellar composition.
explanations.C: Correct. The flagellum is composed of the protein flagellin, arranged in a helical filament. This protein basis is a standard, testable structural fact about the flagellum. It is exactly this filament's rotation that drives the flagellum's motility function.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Adherence to host cells is chiefly the role of pili/fimbriae and the capsule, not the flagellum, whose defining role is motility.

questions.learning_objective: State that the flagellum is protein in nature, rejecting a short/rigid description, LPS composition and an adherence role.

questions.title: F plasmid genes direct sex pilus formation
questions.question: Sex pili formation is function of ?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The ribosome carries out protein synthesis generally; it does not itself encode which appendages a cell forms.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Sex pilus formation is specifically an F-plasmid-encoded trait, not a core chromosomal one.
explanations.C: Correct. The genes directing sex pilus (F pilus) formation are carried on the F (fertility) plasmid. A donor cell possessing this plasmid forms the sex pilus needed to establish contact with a recipient cell during conjugation, the process by which the plasmid itself is transferred.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The cell wall is a structural layer, not the genetic determinant of which surface appendages a cell forms.

questions.learning_objective: State that sex pilus formation is directed by the F plasmid, not the ribosome, chromosome or cell wall.

questions.title: Lipid A is present in Gram-negative but not Gram-positive walls
questions.question: Which of the following is present in cell wall of gram-negative bacteria but not gram-positive bacteria ?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Teichoic acid is the reverse case -- present in the Gram-positive wall, absent from the Gram-negative one.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Peptidoglycan is present in both Gram-positive and Gram-negative walls (thick in the former, thin in the latter), not unique to Gram-negative bacteria.
explanations.C: Correct. Lipid A, the lipid anchor of lipopolysaccharide, is embedded in the outer membrane found only in the Gram-negative cell envelope. Gram-positive bacteria have no outer membrane at all, so they carry no Lipid A. This makes Lipid A a genuine, structurally grounded Gram-negative-specific feature.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Phospholipid is a component of the cytoplasmic membrane shared by both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria, not a Gram-negative-specific wall feature.

questions.learning_objective: Identify Lipid A as present in the Gram-negative but not Gram-positive cell wall, rejecting teichoic acid, peptidoglycan and phospholipid as the distinguishing feature.

questions.title: The capsule protects the organism from phagocytosis
questions.question: Protect the organism from phagocytosis ?

explanations.A: Correct. The polysaccharide (or, in Bacillus anthracis, polypeptide) capsule surrounding many bacteria is a major virulence factor. It resists phagocytosis by host immune cells precisely by physically masking surface molecules that phagocytes would otherwise recognise and bind. This antiphagocytic role is the capsule's defining function.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A spore protects the organism from unfavourable environmental conditions (drying, heat), not specifically from phagocytosis.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Flagella are the organelle of motility; they play no role in resisting phagocytosis.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The cell wall gives shape and rigidity and is a site of antibiotic action; protecting from phagocytosis is specifically the capsule's role, not the wall's.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The cytoplasmic membrane is the selectively permeable barrier and respiratory site; it plays no role in resisting phagocytosis.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the capsule as the structure that protects the organism from phagocytosis, distinct from the spore, flagella, cell wall and cytoplasmic membrane.

questions.title: Mesosomes are cytoplasmic membrane invaginations
questions.question: Mesosomes are ?

explanations.A: Correct. Mesosomes are classically described as invaginations of the cytoplasmic membrane, increasing its effective surface area. This role is broadly analogous to the mitochondrial cristae of a eukaryotic cell. Unlike mitochondria, mesosomes are a bacteria-specific feature with no sterol content.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Mesosomes are membrane, not cell-wall, structures -- a distinct compartment of the bacterial envelope.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Bacteria have no true nucleus, so an "intra-nuclear" structure is not applicable; mesosomes are cytoplasmic membrane features, not nuclear ones.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Mesosomes are not themselves a site of antibiotic action -- the cell wall (peptidoglycan) and ribosomes are the classic antibiotic targets.

questions.learning_objective: State that mesosomes are cytoplasmic membrane invaginations, not a cell-wall, nuclear or antibiotic-target structure.

questions.title: The capsule's function is protection from phagocytosis
questions.question: Function of bacterial capsule is ?

options.A: Protection of bacterial cell from phagocytosis

explanations.A: Correct. The capsule's defining function is antiphagocytic protection, resisting engulfment by host immune cells. It also serves secondary uses in organism identification/serotyping and as a vaccine antigen (e.g. pneumococcal or meningococcal vaccines). Protection from phagocytosis remains the capsule's core, primary role.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Giving shape and rigidity is the cell wall's function, not the capsule's -- the capsule is an outer covering additional to, and distinct from, the wall beneath it.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Selective permeability is a function of the cytoplasmic membrane, not the capsule.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Secretion of hydrolytic enzymes is not the capsule's role; such enzymes are excreted through the cytoplasmic membrane.

questions.learning_objective: State that the capsule's function is protection from phagocytosis, rejecting shape/rigidity, selective permeability and enzyme secretion.

questions.title: The sex pilus mediates gene transfer
questions.question: Sex pili is responsible for ?

explanations.A: Incorrect. General adhesion to surfaces is chiefly the role of ordinary (common) pili and the capsule, not the sex pilus specifically.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Motility is the flagellum's role, not the sex pilus's.
explanations.C: Correct. The sex pilus (F pilus) forms the physical connection between a donor and recipient cell during bacterial conjugation, through which plasmid DNA -- often carrying antibiotic-resistance genes -- is transferred. Gene transfer via conjugation is the sex pilus's defining function.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Bacterial replication (binary fission) is a chromosome-directed process unrelated to the sex pilus's own conjugative role.

questions.learning_objective: Identify gene transfer (conjugation) as the sex pilus's function, distinct from adhesion, motility and replication.

questions.title: Porins in the outer membrane admit small molecules
questions.question: Contain porins that allow passage of small molecules ?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The cell wall's peptidoglycan mesh is not what carries porin channels -- porins are outer-membrane proteins, a distinct structure.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Spores are dormant survival structures, unrelated to porin-mediated molecular transport.
explanations.C: Correct. The outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria carries porin proteins that span it. These porins allow passage of small hydrophilic solutes while excluding larger molecules such as amino acids or proteins. The same outer membrane also carries the toxic Lipid A component of lipopolysaccharide.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The cytoplasmic membrane uses its own dedicated transport proteins for selective permeability; porins specifically are an outer-membrane feature of Gram-negative bacteria, not a cytoplasmic-membrane one.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the outer membrane as the structure carrying porins that admit small molecules, distinct from the cell wall, spores and cytoplasmic membrane.

questions.title: The cell wall does not mediate adherence to surfaces
questions.question: All of the following mediate adherence of bacteria to surfaces EXCEPT ?

explanations.A: Incorrect (genuine adherence mediator, not the EXCEPT). The capsule contributes to surface adherence and biofilm formation alongside its antiphagocytic role.
explanations.B: Incorrect (genuine adherence mediator, not the EXCEPT). Glycocalyx, a loose polysaccharide layer, mediates adherence to surfaces and to host tissue.
explanations.C: Correct. This is the false statement, so it is the EXCEPT answer. The cell wall's defining roles are giving shape and rigidity and serving as a site of antibiotic action; adherence to surfaces is instead mediated by dedicated structures -- the capsule, glycocalyx and ordinary pili -- not the wall itself.
explanations.D: Incorrect (genuine adherence mediator, not the EXCEPT). Ordinary (common) pili are classic adherence structures, allowing bacteria to attach to host cells and surfaces.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the cell wall as the structure that does not mediate surface adherence, while correctly recognising the capsule, glycocalyx and ordinary pili as adherence mediators.

questions.title: Peptidoglycan gives bacteria their rigidity and shape
questions.question: The rigidity and shape of bacteria is due to ?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The cytoplasmic membrane is a fragile phospholipid bilayer, osmotically sensitive on its own -- it relies on the wall outside it for rigidity, not the reverse.
explanations.B: Correct. Peptidoglycan is the cross-linked sugar-peptide mesh forming the structural backbone of the bacterial cell wall. It is this mesh that gives the cell its rigidity and characteristic shape. Peptidoglycan is thick in Gram-positive bacteria and thin in Gram-negative ones, but it is structurally central to both.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Lipopolysaccharide (LPS) is the toxic/antigenic component of the Gram-negative outer membrane, not the structural layer providing shape and rigidity.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Teichoic acid is a Gram-positive wall component contributing to wall charge and immune activation, not the primary rigidity-conferring structure.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The capsule is an outer, often gel-like layer whose role is antiphagocytic protection, not maintaining the cell's rigid shape.

questions.learning_objective: State that peptidoglycan gives bacteria their rigidity and shape, rejecting the cell membrane, LPS, teichoic acid and capsule as the source.

questions.title: Ordinary fimbriae are long, thin protein appendages
questions.question: Which is true regarding ordinary fimbriae ?

options.A: Long, thin appendages made up of protein
options.D: Present mainly in gram negative bacteria

explanations.A: Correct. Ordinary fimbriae (pili) are long, thin, hair-like surface appendages composed of protein subunits. Their role is mediating adherence to host cells and other surfaces. This adherence function is distinct from any of the roles named in the other options.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Gene transfer is the role of the specialised sex pilus during conjugation, not ordinary fimbriae, whose role is adherence.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Motility is the flagellum's role; ordinary fimbriae are non-motile adherence structures.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Fimbriae occur across a range of bacteria, not restricted mainly to Gram-negative organisms.

questions.learning_objective: State that ordinary fimbriae are long, thin protein appendages, rejecting a gene-transfer, motility or Gram-negative-restricted description.

questions.title: Peptidoglycan is the main structure of the Gram-positive cell wall
questions.question: The main structure of the cell wall of gram-positive bacteria ?

explanations.A: Correct. The Gram-positive cell wall is fundamentally a thick, multilayered mesh of peptidoglycan. Teichoic acid is threaded through this mesh as a secondary component. Peptidoglycan itself remains the main structural component of the wall.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Lipopolysaccharide (LPS) is a Gram-negative outer-membrane component; Gram-positive bacteria have no outer membrane and so no LPS at all.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Fatty acids are not the main structural component of the Gram-positive wall -- the peptidoglycan mesh is.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Since LPS and fatty acids are not genuine Gram-positive wall components, "all of the above" incorrectly includes them alongside peptidoglycan.

questions.learning_objective: State that peptidoglycan is the main structure of the Gram-positive cell wall, rejecting LPS, fatty acids and an "all of the above" answer.

questions.title: Mycoplasma is the only prokaryote with membrane sterol
questions.question: The only prokaryotic that have sterol in cell membrane is ?

explanations.A: Correct. Mycoplasma is unique among prokaryotes in incorporating sterols, cholesterol scavenged from the host, directly into its cytoplasmic membrane. This sterol content compensates for Mycoplasma's complete lack of a cell wall. It adds membrane rigidity that the missing wall would otherwise have provided.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Ordinary Gram-positive bacteria have a peptidoglycan cell wall and do not incorporate sterol into their cytoplasmic membrane.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Rickettsia is an obligate intracellular Gram-negative bacterium with a conventional Gram-negative envelope, not a sterol-containing membrane.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Chlamydia is likewise an obligate intracellular Gram-negative-type organism, not one with sterol in its membrane.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Ordinary Gram-negative bacteria have their own outer-membrane/peptidoglycan envelope and do not incorporate sterol into the cytoplasmic membrane.

questions.learning_objective: Identify Mycoplasma as the only prokaryote with sterol in its cell membrane, distinguishing it from Gram-positive bacteria, Rickettsia, Chlamydia and Gram-negative bacteria.

questions.title: Fimbriae contribute to pathogenicity through adhesion
questions.question: Fimbriae contribute to pathogenicity of bacteria by helping in ?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Locomotion is the flagellum's role, not fimbriae, which are non-motile.
explanations.B: Correct. Fimbriae's contribution to pathogenicity is chiefly through adhesion. They attach the bacterium to host cell surfaces, the essential first step in colonisation. Without this adhesion step, many infections could not become established.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Release of hydrolytic/toxic enzymes is not a fimbrial function; it occurs at the cytoplasmic membrane.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Antiphagocytic protection is the capsule's role, not fimbriae's.

questions.learning_objective: State that fimbriae contribute to pathogenicity through adhesion, rejecting locomotion, enzyme release and antiphagocytic roles.

questions.title: Pathogenic bacteria are heterotrophic
questions.question: Pathogenic bacteria are ?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Autotrophs synthesise their own organic nutrients from inorganic sources; pathogenic bacteria instead depend on organic nutrients from their host.
explanations.B: Correct. Pathogenic bacteria are heterotrophic. They obtain their organic carbon and energy needs from their host's own organic compounds rather than synthesising these from inorganic sources. This dependency is consistent with their parasitic lifestyle.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Phototrophic organisms derive energy from light; this describes some environmental bacteria, not host-dependent pathogens.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Psychrophilic describes a cold-loving temperature preference, an unrelated property to the nutritional classification being tested here.

questions.learning_objective: State that pathogenic bacteria are heterotrophic, rejecting autotrophic, phototrophic and psychrophilic descriptions.

questions.title: Mycoplasma is the prokaryote lacking a cell wall
questions.question: All prokaryotes are surrounded by a cell wall EXCEPT ?

explanations.A: Correct. This is the exception, so it is the EXCEPT answer. Mycoplasma genuinely lacks a cell wall entirely -- it compensates by incorporating sterol into its cytoplasmic membrane for structural stability, a unique feature among prokaryotes.
explanations.B: Incorrect (true statement, not the EXCEPT). Spirochetes do have a cell wall, along with their characteristic helical shape and internal axial filaments.
explanations.C: Incorrect (true statement, not the EXCEPT). Actinomycetes are Gram-positive bacteria with a conventional peptidoglycan cell wall.
explanations.D: Incorrect (true statement, not the EXCEPT). Methanogens, though archaea rather than true bacteria, possess a cell wall (of a distinct, non-peptidoglycan composition), so they are not wall-less.

questions.learning_objective: Identify Mycoplasma as the prokaryote lacking a cell wall, rejecting spirochetes, actinomycetes and methanogens as the exception.
